summary: Describes a framework and process for developing performance metrics for protocols and applications carried over IETF protocols. Such metrics characterize traffic on live networks and services. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6390 explains how to define a network performance measurement so different people can collect and interpret it consistently. It also describes how the IETF reviews proposals for new measurements.

subtitle: A framework for defining, documenting and reviewing network performance measurements.

tldr.problem: Measurements cannot be compared reliably when people define or collect them differently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the required and recommended parts of a metric definition and describes a review process involving the Performance Metrics Directorate.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice for developing metrics, not a source of metrics itself. The unit metadata lists no later update or replacement.

today: RFC 6390 is a Best Current Practice published in October 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Standardized Metrics Matter
sections.content:
Network and application performance can be affected by congestion, IP impairments, server capacity and other causes. Measuring performance helps people check service goals and diagnose problems. A shared definition makes measurements more consistent and results easier to compare.

The RFC describes three parts of metric standardization: define the metric and its units, specify how to measure it, and specify how to report it. It focuses on metrics for protocols and applications above and below the IP layer, including measurements on live networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A performance number is useful only when people know what it measures and how it was collected. Shared rules let readers compare results from different measurements.

sections.title: What a Performance Metric Measures
sections.content:
A Performance Metric is a quantitative measure of observable behavior in an IETF-specified protocol or an application carried over one. The RFC gives examples such as the time to download a complete file with FTP or to resolve an address with DNS. This document sets out a process; it does not define any metrics.

Quality of Service (QoS) describes service characteristics that affect whether user needs are met. Quality of Experience (QoE) describes the quality users believe they experienced and includes qualitative factors such as expectations and the task. Application metrics can connect network measurements, such as packet loss and delay, to application behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: A metric is a defined number about a protocol, application or service. QoS describes measurable service behavior, while QoE describes how users judge the service in their situation.

sections.title: Choosing and Assessing a Metric
sections.content:
Metric authors should identify who will use the result and what decision it supports. Users may differ in their need for active or passive measurement, laboratory or live-network measurements, accuracy, measurement locations, scale, sampling and reporting periods.

A metric may be measured directly or calculated from other metrics. A composed metric uses a defined function to combine measurements across time or space. The RFC recommends asking whether a metric adds important information, relates to application performance or user experience, helps locate problems, and supports a policy or service agreement.

The packet loss example shows why a simple average may not answer every question. An application sensitive to bursts may need a measure of how often and how long loss exceeds a threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: First decide who needs the measurement and what they will use it to learn. A single average may hide patterns that matter, such as repeated periods of high packet loss.

sections.title: Required Parts of a Metric Definition
sections.content:
A metric definition MUST explain what is measured and how it is measured or calculated. Its normative part MUST name and describe the metric, specify the method, state the units, identify measurement points and domain where relevant, and define measurement timing and required timing accuracy.

The method should address active versus passive collection, calculation details, exceptions, and when a packet counts as lost rather than delayed. The informative part SHOULD explain implementation, verification, use and applications, and reporting. The RFC's template separates these six required parts from those four recommended supporting parts.
sections.plainLanguage: A definition MUST name the measurement, explain the method and units, identify where it is taken, and say when it is taken. It SHOULD also help readers implement, test, use and report it consistently.

sections.title: Dependencies and Review Process
sections.content:
Metric authors SHOULD document timing accuracy, related events or measurements, lower-layer dependencies, middleboxes and user-set parameters. For example, a measurement that counts events per interval can change when the interval's timing changes. A proxy or network address translator can also restrict what a measurement observes.

Proposals SHOULD be written as Internet-Drafts, fit relevant working-group work, identify their audience, assess overlap with other standards bodies, and identify security and IANA needs. Reviewers SHOULD check that definitions are unambiguous, results repeatable, and errors and assumptions documented. The Performance Metrics Directorate SHALL guide the related working group.
sections.plainLanguage: Metric authors should disclose conditions that can change a result, including timing, network devices and settings. Reviewers check whether people can repeat the method and understand what the result means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framework itself does not create an Internet security issue, but an individual metric can introduce risks. The RFC asks metric authors to identify those risks. Active tests on live networks can be misused, and passive measurements can expose information about users or traffic.

The security considerations for active measurement and for selecting packets during passive measurement also apply. The framework points to RFC 4656 and RFC 5475 for those topics.
sections.plainLanguage: A measurement can reveal information about people or be misused to affect a network. Authors should describe these risks for each metric they define.
